name: Eye color change drops

lead: People discuss drops, including latanoprost-type and homemade ones, to lighten brown eyes toward blue, green or hazel. Iris colour depends largely on the melanin in the iris stroma. No peer-reviewed study has tested a cosmetic drop for lightening. Latanoprost, a glaucoma medicine, is labelled to increase brown iris pigment, so its documented effect runs toward darker eyes.

Forum conversation mostly moves to procedures. Keratopigmentation places pigment in the cornea, laser depigmentation uses a Nd:YAG laser to remove stromal melanin, and implants cover the iris with a coloured artificial disc. Reviews describe keratopigmentation as the best studied option, laser as having limited long-term data and implants as the weakest on safety.

paras: Forum users compare drops, corneal tattooing, laser depigmentation and iris implants, with the procedures done by eye surgeons or clinics abroad. Results from procedures are visible once healed, and forum posters themselves raise contamination concerns about homemade drops.

Reviews report that cosmetic iris implants are not approved by major regulators and have been linked to glaucoma, uveitis, corneal damage and vision loss. Laser depigmentation has limited long-term safety data, and keratopigmentation still lacks long-term cosmetic evidence. Unregulated drops placed in the eye carry general risks of contamination and infection.

angle.text: Users discuss drops, including latanoprost-type and homemade ones, to lighten brown eyes toward blue, green or hazel, alongside keratopigmentation, laser depigmentation and implants. No peer-reviewed study has tested a cosmetic drop for this; latanoprost is documented to darken irises, and surgical routes carry documented eye risks.

lead: Eye color change drops is a term used in looksmaxxing communities for eye drops that are claimed to lighten the color of the iris, usually from brown toward blue, green or hazel. No peer-reviewed study has examined a cosmetic drop for lightening eye color.

The prescription drug most often connected to the topic is latanoprost, a glaucoma medicine whose labelled side effects include increased brown iris pigmentation, meaning it tends to darken rather than lighten eyes. Microscopy studies attribute the change to more melanin inside existing iris melanocytes. [1]

Forum discussion largely moves from drops to procedures. Published reviews describe three surgical approaches to cosmetic eye color change: iris implants, laser iris depigmentation and cosmetic keratopigmentation, with the evidence base strongest for the last and weakest for implants' safety.

paras: The phrase covers several separate things that forum users sometimes conflate: over-the-counter or homemade drops said to lighten the iris, prescription drops that incidentally change iris color, and clinic procedures that change apparent eye color. On looksmax.org, one detailed post by a user who reports having had laser depigmentation says they do not believe in drops, and warns that preparing eye drops without medical training carries a high infection rate. [2]

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue used for glaucoma and ocular hypertension; it is prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia and the EU and was approved in 1996. Increased brown iris pigmentation is listed among its common effects. [3]

A review of iris histology after latanoprost concluded that the darkening is likely due to more melanin within iris stromal melanocytes rather than more melanocytes, and that susceptible individuals, particularly those with hazel eyes, are most affected. The authors noted that numbers of specimens examined were small.  A 3-month randomized study of 17 glaucoma patients found no degenerative or proliferative iris changes, with one case of color change among the treated eyes. [4] An earlier case report examined an iridectomy specimen from a patient with latanoprost-induced color change. [1]
Forum threads ask whether latanoprost or the related eyelash product Latisse can change eye color. [5][6] The published drug literature describes darkening, not lightening.

Keratopigmentation, or corneal tattooing, has a history reaching back to antiquity and was developed in modern form in the 19th century; Francis Ferrari is credited with first using it for cosmetic purposes on healthy eyes, and femtosecond-laser versions are sometimes called FLAAK. Reported risks include fading pigment, corneal erosions, keratitis and ulceration. [7]

A 2025 narrative review describes three main surgical approaches: cosmetic iris implants, laser iris depigmentation and keratopigmentation. It says implants, repurposed from treatment of iris defects, carry severe risks including glaucoma, endothelial cell loss and permanent vision impairment and are widely considered unsafe; laser depigmentation gives a natural look but has potential complications such as patchy pigmentation, photophobia and temporary pressure spikes, with limited long-term data; and keratopigmentation was reported as the safest of the three.

A 2022 review described cosmetic iris implants as lacking CE marking and FDA approval and associated with uveitis, hyphema, glaucoma, cataract and vision loss, and noted that scientific data on laser depigmentation are very limited.  A 2026 review in Cornea reported generally favorable short-term outcomes and high patient satisfaction in selected cases but called for long-term evidence, pigment standardization and careful patient selection.

No studies found on drops sold or made to lighten eye color. Related research covers latanoprost-induced iris darkening in glaucoma patients [4] and surgical cosmetic eye-color procedures, which are described mainly in case series and reviews rather than controlled trials.

Posters on looksmax.org describe lighter eyes as a desirable feature and discuss saving money for clinic procedures abroad, with other posters disputing the quality of particular clinics' results. [5][8] One thread author says some people had reported fake before-and-after images from clinics, and that implant feedback shared online can be dangerous. [2] Another thread quotes a clinic's marketing that it carries no side effects or risks, a statement that differs from the complication profile in published reviews. [8]

lore.intro: Eye color is discussed on looksmax.org as a feature that can be changed, with debate about which method is safe and whether the results look natural. [5][2]

claims.claim: Drops such as latanoprost or Latisse can change eye color.
Homemade or supplement-style drops can lighten the iris.
Keratopigmentation is a safe way to change eye color.
Laser depigmentation permanently and safely lightens eyes with no side effects.
Iris implants are an option for eye color change.
